archetype: Mono-green Draw-Go Stompy: a creature-dense midrange deck whose commander turns every creature into a potential instant, playing ambush-control until the overrun window opens.

role_assignment.default_role: Trap-holding developer. Early and midgame the deck passes with mana open and deploys on other players' turns — verified stack 001 establishes the mechanical basis: Radagast's discount-plus-flash applies to the first creature spell YOU cast each turn, on every player's turn, so a four-player round offers four windows and Wood Elves costs {G} on an opponent's end step. This is the posture strategy:multiplayer.pod-management names directly: 'Leaving instant-speed mana open forces three players, not one, to respect your possible interaction.' The role is seat-relative per strategy:whos-the-beatdown — against a faster combat seat this deck is the control (traps blank their attackers); against control or combo it must be the beatdown, because it does not own the long game against either.
role_assignment.pivot_trigger: The pivot is a countable event, per strategy:pivot-point ('the pivot is usually triggered by a concrete event'): five-plus bodies on board with a mass-pump finisher in hand. Verified stack 003 sets the exact bar — Craterhoof over four bodies (X=5) deals 36 unblocked to one seat, honestly NOT lethal from 40; one more body clears it. So the trigger is bodies ≥5 and a finisher held, taken per strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window: count the table's open mana and hold Heroic Intervention or Tyvar's Stand for the turn you commit. The commitment has a verified shape: the BODIES land on end steps and attack at dawn free of summoning sickness (verified stack 006), but the FINISHER is cast from your own precombat main — stack 005 verifies that a Craterhoof flashed on the end step before yours is legal, resolves, and survives, yet its +X/+X pump ends at that turn's cleanup and contributes nothing to your combat; the flashed Hoof is a wrath-dodge, never the kill (strategy:tempo.sequencing).

engines.engine: The metronome: discount+flash on the first creature spell each turn, recurring on every player's turn — four full-value windows per round, each casting a 3–5 MV body with ≥2 generic at maximum discount. One drawn by t6 in 94.5% of goldfish runs. Yeva, Nature's Herald splits the two permissions: the DISCOUNT stays once per turn (Radagast prices the first creature spell), but with Yeva out the TIMING permission is deck-wide — every green creature spell has flash, so a window can hold a second body at retail. The end-step body wakes ready either way: a creature flashed the turn before yours attacks and taps freely, both prongs of rule 302.6 verified (stack 006) — flash deployment costs nothing in tempo.

Flash traps — interaction wearing creature bodies. Stack 002 verifies the flagship line: Frostfang flashed after blockers are declared applies deathtouch to combat damage already lined up, and its attack trigger draws two off one unblocked 1/1 plus indestructible Toski. The class (Nantuko Vigilante, Wickerbough Elder, Indrik Stomphowler, Caustic Caterpillar, Heroic Intervention, Veil of Summer, Tyvar's Stand, Chord of Calling, Guardian Augmenter, and Whiptongue Hydra — a flashable 4/4 reach whose ETB wipes every flier) is drawn by t6 at 91.3%. Chord is the trap that refuses Radagast's gifts — verified stack 007: it takes no discount and no flash window (it is an instant, not a creature spell), Castle Garenbrig's six-mana burst cannot pay it, and the fetched body triggers no Beast Whisperer draw; only Garenbrig's plain {T}: Add {G} helps, and X=3 fetches Selvala at instant speed. Every open {G}{G} is also a bluff the whole table must price (strategy:information: 'opponents who must respect tricks play slower and worse').

Per-cast gas: Beast Whisperer, Tribute to the World Tree, Toski, Selvala, Garruk's Uprising, Elemental Bond, Fecundity, Harmonize, and Glademuse — whose 'if it's not their turn' clause is tuned to this deck exactly: every flashed body on an opponent's turn draws a card. Repeatable draw keyed to the thing the deck does anyway (casting creatures, often twice a round). GAS drawn by t6 at 75.9%. This is the format-defining shape per strategy:card-advantage: 'engines that out-draw three players are the format's defining advantage.' Stack 004 verifies the grimmest mode: under Day of Judgment, Fecundity is symmetric, tokens trigger it, indestructible Toski skips the wake, and the commander's death is seen before he moves to the command zone — the wrath itself refills the hand.

Two-humped ramp: eight 1-MV dork-class accelerants plus seven land-ramp spells plus aura ramp (Utopia Sprawl, Wild Growth, Fertile Ground) — 17+ cards, RAMP drawn by t6 at 93.6%, commander mean cast t4.02 and 94.1% by t6. Redundancy over tutors, per strategy:deckbuilding.redundancy-vs-tutors: 'stack the classes you want every game (ramp, draw, removal, enablers), tutor only the irreplaceable' — at ~17 copies the class clears the 54%-of-openers band the doc prices for 10 copies with room to spare.
engines.evidence: goldfish_metrics; mana_analysis (G36 sources, 90.6% lands-only on-curve, 97.0% with dorks)

engines.engine: Commander insurance: Guardian Augmenter (flashed, grants the commander hexproof +2/+2), Heroic Intervention, Tyvar's Stand, Veil of Summer, Sylvan Safekeeper — and Yeva, Nature's Herald as functional insurance of a different kind: a second flash enabler (herself flash), so answering Radagast no longer answers the deck's identity, only its discount. The whole deck is linear on Radagast's window, and strategy:critical-mass names the price: 'sequence so one removal spell can't break the chain' — the linear deck's defense is 'speed, redundancy, and resilience, not answers.' Without Radagast the deck is fair stompy at retail prices; the insurance class keeps the threshold protected.
engines.evidence: oracle text (cards.json); goldfish flash-trap group includes the protection suite

engines.engine: The overrun kill: Craterhoof, Overwhelming Stampede, Pathbreaker Ibex, Return of the Wildspeaker — four finishers, exactly the 3–5 band strategy:deckbuilding.threat-density sets ('at least 3 finishers in your deck'). The wide alpha strike is the payoff that scales against ~120 combined life, per strategy:multiplayer.asymmetry: 'wide alpha strikes, loops, commander-damage kills, and each-opponent drains are the payoffs that actually scale.' Stack 003 verifies the arithmetic honestly: X=5 over four bodies is 36 into one seat — a finisher needs the board the bodies rates price separately (finisher+second-wave assembled by t6: 40.2%). The kill line is cast from your own precombat main: stack 005 verifies that a Hoof flashed on the prior end step loses its pump at that turn's cleanup — Craterhoof's own haste makes the main-phase cast lose nothing, and the flash mode is reserved for dodging a telegraphed wrath.
engines.evidence: verified stack 003; verified stack 005; goldfish_metrics (finisher drawn 42.4% by t6 unassisted)

candidate_missing_lines.title: Selvala into the flashed giant: does the metronome feed her draw and mana
candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: Oracle text: Selvala draws whenever a creature with the highest power enters, and taps for mana equal to the greatest power among creatures you control — flashed 3–5 MV bodies on every player's turn are repeated triggers, and she is the declared big-mana-sink route. She is also the sim's single one-card class (drawn 16.3% overall, no functional backup in the 99), though Chord at X=3 fetches her at instant speed (verified stack 007). Her draw trigger wants a greatest-power entrance, which Whiptongue Hydra (4/4 and growing) or Craterhoof carries. Whether her mana can pay a flashed cast in the same window is unverified.

matchup_frames.vs_sweeper_control: The best matchup shape the deck's mechanics allow, and stack 004 is the proof of concept: Fecundity converts the wrath into a hand for you (your four wakes to their one), Toski survives it outright, and the commander insurance suite holds Radagast through targeted attempts. Play strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math exactly as written — 'commit exactly as much as wins before it arrives, no further,' and 'buy resilience instead of restraint': flash deployment IS the resilience, because bodies cast on the end step after a wrath window closes were never exposed to it — and they attack at dawn regardless (verified stack 006). Against the telegraphed sweeper, even Craterhoof can be flash-deployed purely to dodge it (verified stack 005: legal, resolves, survives — but the pump dies at that turn's cleanup, so the overrun still waits for your own main). Redeploy worst-first after the sweep, keeping the finisher for their second one.
matchup_frames.vs_stax: The deck is many cheap creature spells per turn — the profile strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial says taxes hit hardest ('taxes attack the velocity math directly, so recount your hand under the tax'). Radagast's {2} discount partially rebates one tax on one spell per turn, but the doc's role rule binds: 'you rarely own the long game under an assembling lock, so you are the beatdown.' Name the out early — Boseiju, Beast Within, Caustic Caterpillar, Wickerbough Elder, Nantuko Vigilante break the piece that beats YOU — and note Collector Ouphe is this deck's own stax piece against artifact-mana tables.
matchup_frames.vs_aggro: Seat-relative control, per strategy:whos-the-beatdown's Commander correction. The traps are the plan: stack 002 verifies that Frostfang after blockers turns every lined-up blocker lethal, and strategy:card-advantage.virtual names the mechanism — 'a big blocker against an aggro deck turns their small creatures into dead cards.' Radagast's own 2/5 body, Whiptongue Hydra — flashed as a 4/4 reach blocker whose ETB destroys every flier, the one board wipe mono-green combat decks are supposed to lack — and the deathtouch grant make attacking into open green mana unprofitable for three seats at once, on the ground or in the air. Let the aggro seat spend itself on the table, then pivot the turn you stabilize — 'once you stabilize, every extra passive turn is a free draw step for the opponent' (strategy:pivot-point).
matchup_frames.vs_combo: You are the beatdown — the deck holds zero counterspells (Veil of Summer answers only blue/black targeting) and cannot win the long game against inevitability, so per strategy:whos-the-beatdown 'whoever loses the long game must be the beatdown.' The clock must be honest about its own arithmetic: stack 003 says one overrun into one seat from 40 needs five bodies, so combo assessment per strategy:threat-assessment ranks the combo player's proximity above every board. Creature-shaped interaction (Collector Ouphe against artifact combo, Caustic Caterpillar, Boseiju) flashed on the combo player's upkeep is the only disruption; spend it on the piece that wins, not the piece that impresses.

distribution_notes: 36 lands (30 basics — mana_analysis: G36 sources against a G36 target, 90.6% lands-only on-curve, 97.0% counting dorks; the cleanest manabase a deck can have) over 64 spells. The curve is two-humped by design and deck-facts shows it: 12 at MV1 (the dork hump), 22 at MV3 (the metronome hump), then a deliberate taper — 5/2/1/1 across MV5-8, because the finishers are few and the doc's threat-density floor (3-5) is met at exactly four. Role histogram: 40 threat:body (the critical mass), 9 draw:engine, 18 ramp across five sub-roles, 10 removal-class entries clearing the brief's ≥5 breadth floor across artifact/enchantment/creature (an artifact-or-enchantment answer drawn by t6 in 63.0% of runs). Goldfish (10k seeded runs): commander mean t4.02, 94.1% by t6 — with keep-7 at 81.5% and mean mulligans 0.22. Bodies on board t6: 3.77 (5.31 by t8) — still short of stack 003's five-body bar, and this is where the sim's three declared blind spots bind: it models neither Radagast's discount, nor opponent-turn flash casts, nor aura ramp, so every rate is a floor for a deck whose whole design is spending mana on other players' turns. Contained combos: zero — bracket_report floor 1 against a target of 3, within target, no game changers, no tutable compression. Four cards have no role entry (three ramp auras and Overwhelming Stampede); absence of a role is not absence of the function.
overall_assessment: This deck is playing the game strategy:multiplayer.pod-management describes in one sentence — 'Leaving instant-speed mana open forces three players, not one, to respect your possible interaction' — and it has built an entire 99 around making that sentence literally true four times a round. The world-view: pass with mana up, deploy a discounted body in whichever of the four windows the table least wants it, draw a card for the trouble, and let the traps make combat against you a losing proposition until five bodies and a finisher assemble; then take the pivot once, protected, from your own precombat main — the bodies having landed on end steps and waking ready to attack (stack 006), the finisher cast where its pump lives to combat (stack 005 bounds the flashed Hoof to a wrath-dodge: the pump dies at that turn's cleanup). It is a linear deck by strategy:critical-mass's definition — every card feeds the metronome, and its defense is redundancy (15 bodies, 17 ramp, 8 gas engines) and insurance rather than answers — wearing a deflection posture the doc explicitly endorses for linear decks in multiplayer ('a deflection posture that keeps them unspent'). Its honest weaknesses are equally legible: the kill needs a board the goldfish says arrives at 3.77 bodies by t6 (a floor, but the bar is 5), Selvala is a declared single point of failure at 16.3%, and combo inevitability is answered by exactly nothing but the clock. All of this is pre-flight: seven checker-passed stacks and 10,000 goldfish runs, zero games played. The frames above are what the artifacts support; the pod will grade them.
gaps: No section on rattlesnake/deterrence theory — visible open mana and trap density as a standing tax on the whole table's attacks is this deck's core defensive mechanism, and the doc reaches it only via one sentence in strategy:multiplayer.pod-management and the bluffing frame in strategy:information. The classic multiplayer archetype literature (rattlesnake cards) deserves its own child section.

No section on flash/draw-go as a multiplayer archetype — instant-speed deployment as deck identity (when to break the draw-go posture, how the table's wrath timing changes when your board grows on end steps) is distinct from 1v1 draw-go control and undocumented.
No section on mono-colour construction tradeoffs — utility lands vs basics when colour is free, and how a zero-fixing manabase changes the ramp package's job.
